args.text:
"Like I've told ya before," says Jeff Peters, "I never had much faith in the perfidiousness of women. As partners, or co-workers in even the most harmless little lurk, you can't trust 'em as far as you can throw 'em."

"That's a compliment they've earned," says I. "Reckon they're entitled to be called the honest sex."

"Course they are," says Jeff. "Why wouldn't they be? They've got the rest of us blokes either on the take or staying back at the office for 'em. They're all right in business, mind, till their feelings or their hair get touched up a bit too much. Then you want a flat-footed, puffing and blowing sort of bloke with sandy whiskers, five nippers, sticky fingers and all, and a building and loan mortgage, waiting in the wings to take over her desk. Now, that puts me in mind of the widow lady me and Andy Tucker took on to help us with that little marriage agency lurk we cooked up out in Cairo.

"See, when you've got enough capital for the advertising--a roll about as fat as the skinny end of a wagon tongue, say--there's good dosh in marriage agencies. We had about $6,000 and we were banking on doubling it in two months, which is about as long as a racket like ours lasts before you'd need to go and take out a New Jersey charter.

"So we knocked up an ad that went more or less like this:

"Charming widow, beautiful, home loving, 32 years, possessing $3,000 cash and owning valuable country property, would remarry. Would prefer a poor man with affectionate disposition to one with means, as she realises that the solid virtues are oftenest to be found in the humble walks of life. No objection to elderly man or one of homely appearance if faithful and true and competent to manage property and invest money with judgment. Address, with particulars.

Lonely, Care of Peters & Tucker, agents, Cairo, Ill.

"'So far, so pernicious,' says I, once we'd finished cooking up our little masterpiece. 'And now,' says I, 'where's the lady?'

"And Andy gives me one of his looks. Dead calm on top, and fed up to the back teeth underneath.

"'Jeff,' he goes, 'I thought you'd chucked in all that realism caper in your art. Why's there gotta be a lady? When they flog heaps of watered stock on Wall Street, do you go looking for a mermaid in it? What's a marriage ad got to do with a lady, ay?'

"'Now you listen here,' says I. 'You know my rule, Andy. In all my shonky little raids on the letter of the law, whatever you're flogging has got to be real: you can see it, you can touch it, you can trot it out. That's how, with a good hard squiz at the council by-laws and the train timetables, I've kept clear of any strife with the cops that a five dollar note and a cigar couldn't square away. So to work this scheme we've got to be able to produce a charming widow in the flesh, or something near enough, with or without the beauty, hereditaments and appurtenances set out in the catalogue and writ of errors. Otherwise we end up held by a justice of the peace, and that's the whole box and dice gone.'

"'Well,' says Andy, and you could see the cogs turning while he put his noggin back together, 'maybe it'd be safer, in case the post office or the peace commission comes sniffing round the agency. But where,' he goes, 'are you gonna find a widow who'd waste her time on a marriage racket with no marriage in it?'

"I told Andy I reckoned I knew just the sheila. Old mate of mine, Zeke Trotter, used to pull soda water and teeth in a tent show. A year back he'd made his missus a widow by knocking back a bottle of the old doctor's indigestion cure instead of the liniment he always got sloshed on. Wrong bottle, poor bugger. I used to drop round their place a fair bit, and I thought we could get her in on it.

"It was only sixty miles to the little town where she lived, so I jumped on the I. C., and there she is, same cottage, same sunflowers, same roosters standing on the washtub. Mrs. Trotter fitted our ad first rate, give or take the beauty and the age and what the property was worth. But she looked workable and respectable enough to the eye, and giving her the job was a kindness to Zeke's memory, rest his soul.
